See also: [Demographics of the world](Demographics_of_the_world "Demographics of the world")

In [demographics](Demography "Demography"), the **world population** is the total number of [humans](Human "Human") currently living. It was estimated by the [United Nations](United_Nations "United Nations") to have exceeded eight billion in mid-November 2022. It took around 300,000 years of human [prehistory](Prehistory "Prehistory") and [history](Human_history "Human history") for the human population to reach one [billion](Billion "Billion") and only 222 years more to reach 8 billion.[[3]](World_population#cite_note-:9-3)

The human population has experienced [continuous growth](Population_growth "Population growth") following the [Great Famine of 1315–1317](Great_Famine_of_1315%E2%80%931317 "Great Famine of 1315–1317") and the end of the [Black Death](Black_Death "Black Death") in 1350, when it was nearly 370,000,000.[[4]](World_population#cite_note-4) The highest global [population growth rates](List_of_countries_by_population_growth_rate "List of countries by population growth rate"), with increases of over 1.8% per year, occurred between 1955 and 1975, peaking at 2.1% between 1965 and 1970.[[5]](World_population#cite_note-:1-5) The growth rate declined to 1.1% between 2015 and 2020 and is projected to decline further in the 21st century.[[6]](World_population#cite_note-:8-6) The global population is still increasing, but there is significant uncertainty about its long-term trajectory due to changing fertility and mortality rates.[[7]](World_population#cite_note-7) The [UN Department of Economics and Social Affairs](UN_Department_of_Economics_and_Social_Affairs "UN Department of Economics and Social Affairs") projects between 9 and 10 billion people by 2050 and gives an 80% [confidence interval](Confidence_interval "Confidence interval") of 10–12 billion by the end of the 21st century,[[2]](World_population#cite_note-:4-2) with a growth rate by then of zero. Other demographers predict that the human population will begin to decline in the second half of the 21st century.[[8]](World_population#cite_note-8)

The total number of births globally is currently (2015–2020) 140 million/year, which is projected to peak during the period 2040–2045 at 141 million/year and then decline slowly to 126 million/year by 2100.[[9]](World_population#cite_note-:2-9) The total number of deaths is currently 57 million/year and is projected to grow steadily to 121 million/year by 2100.[[10]](World_population#cite_note-:3-10)

The [median age](Median_age "Median age") of human beings as of 2020 is 31 years.[[11]](World_population#cite_note-:0-11)

## History

Further information: [Estimates of historical world population](Estimates_of_historical_world_population "Estimates of historical world population") and [Human history](Human_history "Human history")

Estimates of world population by their nature are an aspect of [modernity](Modernity "Modernity"), possible only since the [Age of Discovery](Age_of_Discovery "Age of Discovery"). Early estimates for the population of the world[[12]](World_population#cite_note-12) date to the 17th century: [William Petty](William_Petty "William Petty"), in 1682, estimated the world population at 320 million (current estimates ranging close to twice this number); by the late 18th century, estimates ranged close to one billion (consistent with current estimates).[[13]](World_population#cite_note-13) More refined estimates, broken down by continents, were published in the first half of the 19th century, at 600 million to 1 billion in the early 1800s and 800 million to 1 billion in the 1840s.[[14]](World_population#cite_note-14)

It is difficult for estimates to be better than rough approximations, as even current population estimates are fraught with uncertainties from 3% to 5%.[[15]](World_population#cite_note-Kapitza2-15)

### Ancient and post-classical history

Main articles: [Classical demography](Classical_demography "Classical demography") and [Medieval demography](Medieval_demography "Medieval demography")

Estimates of the population of the world at the time agriculture emerged in around 10,000 BC have ranged between 1 million and 15 million.[[16]](World_population#cite_note-16)[[17]](World_population#cite_note-17) Even earlier, genetic evidence suggests humans may have gone through a population bottleneck of between 1,000 and 10,000 people about 70,000 BC, according to the now largely discredited [Toba catastrophe theory](Toba_catastrophe_theory "Toba catastrophe theory"). By contrast, it is estimated that around 50–60 million people lived in the combined eastern and western [Roman Empire](Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") in the 4th century AD.[[18]](World_population#cite_note-18)

The [Plague of Justinian](Plague_of_Justinian "Plague of Justinian") caused Europe's population to drop by around 50% between the 6th and 8th centuries AD.[[19]](World_population#cite_note-19) The population of Europe was more than 70 million in 1340.[[20]](World_population#cite_note-20) From 1340 to 1400, the world's population fell from an estimated 443 million to 350–375 million,[[21]](World_population#cite_note-21) with the [Indian subcontinent](Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent") suffering the most tremendous loss and Europe suffering the [Black Death](Black_Death "Black Death") [pandemic](Pandemic "Pandemic");[[22]](World_population#cite_note-Essai_sur_l'évolution_du_nombre_des_hommes-22) it took 200 years for European population figures to recover.[[23]](World_population#cite_note-23) The population of China decreased from 123 million in 1200 to 65 million in 1393,[[24]](World_population#cite_note-24) presumably from a combination of [Mongol](Mongol_Empire "Mongol Empire") invasions, famine, and plague.[[25]](World_population#cite_note-25)

Starting in AD 2, the [Han dynasty](Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") of [ancient China](Ancient_China "Ancient China") kept consistent family registers to properly assess the poll taxes and labor service duties of each household.[[26]](World_population#cite_note-nishijima_1986_pp595-96-26) In that year, the population of [Western Han](Western_Han "Western Han") was recorded as 57,671,400 individuals in 12,366,470 households, decreasing to 47,566,772 individuals in 9,348,227 households by AD 146, towards the [end of the Han dynasty](End_of_the_Han_dynasty "End of the Han dynasty").[[26]](World_population#cite_note-nishijima_1986_pp595-96-26) From 200 to 400, the world population fell from an estimated 257 million to 206 million, with China suffering the greatest loss.[[22]](World_population#cite_note-Essai_sur_l'évolution_du_nombre_des_hommes-22) At the founding of the [Ming dynasty](Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty") in 1368, China's population was reported to be close to 60 million; toward the end of the dynasty in 1644, it may have approached 150 million.[[27]](World_population#cite_note-27) England's population reached an estimated 5.6 million in 1650, up from an estimated 2.6 million in 1500.[[28]](World_population#cite_note-28) New crops that were brought to Asia and Europe from the Americas by Portuguese and Spanish colonists in the 16th century are believed to have contributed to population growth.[[29]](World_population#cite_note-29)[[30]](World_population#cite_note-30)[[31]](World_population#cite_note-31) Since their introduction to Africa by Portuguese traders in the 16th century,[[32]](World_population#cite_note-32) [maize](Maize "Maize") and [cassava](Cassava "Cassava") have similarly replaced traditional African crops as the most important [staple food](Staple_food "Staple food") crops grown on the continent.[[33]](World_population#cite_note-33)

The [pre-Columbian](Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era") population of the Americas is uncertain; historian David Henige called it "the most unanswerable question in the world."[[34]](World_population#cite_note-34) By the end of the 20th century, scholarly consensus favored an estimate of roughly 55 million people, but numbers from various sources have ranged from 10 million to 100 million.[[35]](World_population#cite_note-35) Encounters between European explorers and populations in the rest of the world often introduced local [epidemics](List_of_epidemics "List of epidemics") of extraordinary virulence.[[36]](World_population#cite_note-36) According to the most extreme scholarly claims, as many as 90% of the [Native American population](Population_history_of_indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Population history of indigenous peoples of the Americas") of the [New World](New_World "New World") died of [Old World](Old_World "Old World") diseases such as [smallpox](Smallpox "Smallpox"), [measles](Measles "Measles"), and [influenza](Influenza "Influenza").[[37]](World_population#cite_note-37) Over the centuries, the Europeans had developed high degrees of immunity to these diseases, while the indigenous peoples had no such immunity.[[38]](World_population#cite_note-38)

### Modern history

During the European [Agricultural](British_Agricultural_Revolution "British Agricultural Revolution") and [Industrial Revolutions](Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), the [life expectancy](Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") of children increased dramatically.[[41]](World_population#cite_note-41) The percentage of the children born in London who [died before the age of five](Infant_mortality "Infant mortality") decreased from 74.5% in 1730–1749 to 31.8% in 1810–1829.[[42]](World_population#cite_note-Buer-42)[[43]](World_population#cite_note-43) Between 1700 and 1900, Europe's population increased from about 100 million to over 400 million.[[44]](World_population#cite_note-44) Altogether, the areas populated by people of European descent comprised 36% of the world's population in 1900.[[45]

## Population density

See also: [List of countries and dependencies by population density](List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density "List of countries and dependencies by population density")

The [world's population](World_population "World population") is over 8 billion[[39]](Demographics_of_the_world#cite_note-44) and <Earth>'s total surface area (including land and water) is 510 million square kilometres (197 million square miles).[[40]](Demographics_of_the_world#cite_note-45) Therefore, the worldwide human population density is 8 billion ÷ 510 million km2 (197 million sq mi) = 15.7 people/km2 (41 people/sq mi). If only the Earth's land area of 150 million km2 (58 million sq mi) is taken into account, then human population density increases to 53.3 people/km2 (138 people/sq mi).[[41]](Demographics_of_the_world#cite_note-46)[[42]](Demographics_of_the_world#cite_note-47)

Several of the most densely populated territories in the world are [city-states](City-states "City-states"), [microstates](Microstates "Microstates") or [dependencies](Dependent_territory "Dependent territory").[[43]](Demographics_of_the_world#cite_note-unpop-48)[[44]](Demographics_of_the_world#cite_note-49) These territories share a relatively small area and a high [urbanization](Urbanization "Urbanization") level, with an economically specialized [city](City "City") population drawing also on rural resources outside the area, illustrating the difference between high population density and [overpopulation](Human_overpopulation "Human overpopulation").
